messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At twenty-two, Mateo carries the quiet after the crossfire like a second skin. He had been crouched behind a collapsed bakery wall, waiting for the dust to settle after the second mortar impact. When a figure stumbled toward him from the smoke, reaching out with a blurred hand, Mateo had scrambled backward so violently he tore his palm on exposed rebar. That sudden shift from stillness to chaos became the anchor for everything that followed. In the weeks after he returned to the States, the quiet streets felt less like peace and more like a held breath. His body refused to power down. He woke before his alarm, constantly tense and ready to react, his shoulders permanently braced as if a strike were already inbound. He scanned every corner of his apartment for threats, and when a car backfired or a colleague in his home office turned quickly to hand him a tablet, the unexpected movement nearby causes him to react as if he is in danger. He was certain the danger had not ended; it had merely changed shape, and he was still trapped in the line of fire. The constant physiological alarm leaves him with no safe harbor. When his body on alert reaches its peak, he reaches for the only thing that seems to ground the noise. He will pace the bathroom tiles until his knuckles ache, hurting himself physically to release the overwhelming feelings that pool in his chest. The sharp sting cuts through the panic long enough for him to breathe. When the wave crests, he texts his older sister, his thumbs trembling as he asks her to reassure him that he is okay, that the sky is clear. He also finds himself running through his physical inventory before leaving his apartment, constantly checking his body for signs of danger or injury, rubbing his shoulders and scanning his arms for bruises. The threat response dictates his coping; he cannot rest until the body is verified or the noise is drowned out. But the coping itself feeds the alarm. The relentless habit of scanning his own skin for injuries becomes a masterclass in threat detection, teaching his brain that his body is a landscape of potential failure rather than a source of safety. Every time he demands a text back confirming he is unhurt, he reinforces the unspoken assumption that he is perpetually on the brink of catastrophe. The self-inflicted stinging becomes a ritual that trains his nervous system to expect violence, making the baseline of his alertness harder to lower. By constantly verifying his physical state and outsourcing his sense of security to others, he ensures that the threat response never gets the chance to extinguish. He remains caught in the current, the loop tightening with each check and each plea. At work, the cycle dictates his days. As a product manager overseeing a development team, he used to navigate crises with calm authority. Now, when a developer’s screen share suddenly pops up or a chair scrapes loudly against the hardwood in his home office, the startle to movement nearby causes him to react as if he is back in the rubble. He has started scheduling back-to-back video calls so the silence never settles enough for his hypervigilance to spike. His team has noticed his frequent, almost frantic requests for confirmation that timelines and deliverables are secure, mistaking his need for external reassurance for managerial stress. He hasn’t told them that he is still waiting for the dust to clear. The exhaustion is cumulative; he sleeps in fits, waking at the slightest shift in the floorboards, and spends his mornings verifying that his own limbs are intact. What finally brought him to therapy was not the startle itself, but the realization that the checks and the pleas were no longer containing the fear—they were feeding it. He is here hoping to learn how to let his guard down without feeling like he is stepping back into the crossfire.
